content.page_summary: Discussion of Type 2 myocardial infarction (Type 2 MI) and myocardial injury, their causes, diagnostic considerations, and complications (including heart failure) with emphasis on differences from Type 1 MI and management principles.
content.definitions: Type 2 MI is an ischaemic myocardial injury in the context of a mismatch between oxygen supply and demand not related to acute coronary atherothrombosis. Myocardial injury is characterized by myocyte necrosis and troponin elevation due to mechanisms other than myocardial ischaemia and can be acute or chronic.
causes_of_Type_2_MI: Non-coronary mechanisms: hypoxia, hypotension, anaemia, tachycardia, bradycardia
diagnostic_points: Distinction between Type 1 and Type 2 MI is important; an algorithmic approach is recommended.
High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) assays detect myocardial injury but are not specific for MI.
Patients with elevated hs-cTn without evidence of acute myocardial ischaemia may be diagnosed with myocardial injury; diagnosis can change if subsequent investigations meet MI criteria.

After stabilization and treatment of precipitating illness, targeted echocardiography and/or coronary angiography (invasive or CCTA) can identify contributory cardiac conditions and guide long-term treatment.
management_recommendations: No specific pharmacological interventions are currently recommended specifically for Type 2 MI due to lack of robust evidence.
Management should focus on identifying and treating precipitating conditions (e.g., anaemia, hypoxia) and strict control of cardiovascular risk factors.
Stabilize patients and treat precipitating illnesses before further diagnostic evaluation.
content.evidence_notes: Due to limited robust scientific evidence on management strategies and wide range of precipitants, no specific recommended pharmacological interventions exist for Type 2 MI.

complications.overview: Type 2 MI and myocardial injury can lead to complications; heart failure (HF) is a key complication discussed.

heart_failure.description: Acute HF may occur as a complication of acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Acute HF resulting from ACS increases risk of in-hospital complications (worsening renal function, respiratory failure, pneumonia, death). De novo acute HF complicating ACS should be distinguished from pre-existing HF exacerbated by ACS.
heart_failure.clinical_implications: Presence of acute HF can impede straightforward diagnosis of ACS. Patients with ACS and acute HF are more likely to present with resting dyspnoea and signs/symptoms of fluid overload.

content.clinical_advice_summary: Use algorithmic diagnostic approach to distinguish Type 1 vs Type 2 MI; employ imaging/angiography after stabilization to identify contributory cardiac disease; prioritize treatment of underlying precipitating factors and CV risk control rather than disease-specific pharmacotherapy for Type 2 MI.
